ledger.note: 540: Gwynedd is on the map. ledger.note: 633: Cadwallon holds Northumbria. 'Cadwallon and Penda went and did for the whole land of Northumbria' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, 633) and Bede says he ruled 'the provinces of the Northumbrians' for a year, tyrannically; drawn hatched, never annexed.

region.text: the Northumbrian provinces

ledger.note: 634: Oswald defeats Cadwallon at Heavenfield and Northumbria is free. The page dates Cadwallon's death at 'Denis's-brook' to 634 (some say 633).

region.text: the Dee plain, Flintshire and the Vale of Clwyd, the cells Cliopatria drops in 705

ledger.note: 705: the Dee plain and Vale of Clwyd pass to Mercia. Cliopatria's shape loses seven cells (1,770 km2: Flintshire, Wrexham, the Chester cell and the Vale of Clwyd) while its Mercia row borders Gwynedd 661-829; the page dates no such loss (page silent) and says only that the Welsh kingdoms fought Northumbria and Mercia in 'ongoing warfare' and that the border is 'broadly followed by Offa's Dyke, a late eighth-century earthwork'. Re-checked 2026-10-25 on the Mercia page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercia): silent on 705 and on any Gwynedd land lost to Mercia; it says only that the Meresaete near Chester, 'roughly corresponding to northern Shropshire, Flintshire and Cheshire', were 'under Mercian control from the 7th century' (Tribal Hidage). The year stays a bridge.

c. 825: Merfyn Frych founds the House of Aberffraw. The page: the House of Cunedda ended in the male line with Hywel ap Rhodri Molwynog c. 825; Merfyn's principal court on Anglesey gave the new dynasty its name. Same state, same colour.

region.text: Powys, which Rhodri inherited from his maternal uncle Cyngen

The Powys page has Cyngen die in 854; the Rhodri Mawr page dates no acquisition and quotes Charles-Edwards that Rhodri did not expand beyond Gwynedd's traditional borders. region.text: Seisyllwg (Ceredigion), Gwgon's kingdom

ledger.note: 872: Rhodri takes Seisyllwg. The page: after Gwgon of Seisyllwg drowned without an heir Rhodri took control of the kingdom and installed his son Cadell as a subject king. The Rhodri Mawr page dates Gwgon's drowning to 872 and notes Ben Guy's view that Rhodri may only have been Gwgon's overlord. Cliopatria starts the shape in 875. region.text: Deheubarth and the south-west, which Cliopatria still holds in its Brythons row in 1055

ledger.note: 1055: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn conquers the south. 'In 1055 Gruffudd ap Llywelyn killed his rival Gruffudd ap Rhydderch in battle and recaptured Deheubarth.' Around 1055 he held 'extensive territories along the border with England'. John Davies calls him 'The only Welsh king ever to rule over the entire territory of Wales'.

region.text: Gwent, between the Wye and the Usk

ledger.note: 1055: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn takes Gwent. Around the same time he seized Morgannwg and Gwent along with border territories; the page gives no separate year.

region.text: Morgannwg (Glywysing), Glamorgan

ledger.note: 1055: Gruffudd ap Llywelyn takes Morgannwg (he seized Morgannwg and Gwent at about the same time).

region.text: Brycheiniog, around Brecon

ledger.note: 1055: Brycheiniog is inside Gruffudd's Wales. The page names Deheubarth, Morgannwg and Gwent but not Brycheiniog (page silent); Cliopatria has no Brycheiniog shape 1056-1065 and counts its cells in Gwynedd's 1056 shape. Re-checked 2026-10-25 on the Brycheiniog page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brycheiniog): it has nothing on 1055-1063 or on Gruffydd ap Llywelyn's rule there, so the year stays Cliopatria's.

intersect.text: south Wales: the 47 cells Cliopatria adds in 1056 (Deheubarth, Brycheiniog, Gwent and Morgannwg)

region.text: Deheubarth and the south-west, which Cliopatria still holds in its Brythons row in 1055

ledger.note: 1063: Gruffudd dies and the south is free. He died in Snowdonia in 1063 (the Annals of Ulster say 1064 and name Cynan as killer); the page does not say who took Deheubarth, which Cliopatria's Brythons row holds from 1066.

region.text: Gwent

ledger.note: 1063: Gwent returns to its own line. The page is silent on the south after Gruffudd's death; the Gwent dossier (Kingdom of Gwent page) has Caradog ap Gruffudd re-establish an independent Gwent in 1063.

region.text: Morgannwg (Glywysing)

ledger.note: 1063: Morgannwg returns to its own line (the Glywysing page has the native line under Caradog ap Gruffudd regain Glywysing); this page is silent on the south.

region.text: Brycheiniog

ledger.note: 1063: Brycheiniog leaves Gruffudd's realm with the rest of the south (page silent); Cliopatria's Brycheiniog row resumes in 1066. Re-checked 2026-10-25 on the Brycheiniog page: no entry for 1063, so the year stays Cliopatria's.

region.text: Powys, the Mathrafal line

ledger.note: 1063: Powys goes to the line of Bleddyn. Bleddyn ap Cynfyn and Rhiwallon ap Cynfyn 'came to an agreement with Harold' and were given rule of Gwynedd and Powys; the Powys dossier draws Powys as its own state from 1063 and Cliopatria's Gwynedd shape keeps it to 1084.

1063: Bleddyn and Rhiwallon ap Cynfyn, brothers of the Powys line, take Gwynedd after Gruffudd ap Llywelyn's death and agree terms with Harold. Same state, same colour; the Aberffraw line returns in 1081.
1081: Gruffudd ap Cynan restores the Aberffraw line. The page: he defeated Trahaearn ap Caradog at the Battle of Mynydd Carn and restored the Aberffraw line.

region.text: Gwynedd, 1085-1093 shape

ledger.note: 1094: the Normans hold Gwynedd. The page: Earl Hugh of Chester's forces reached Llyn by 1090 and by 1094 most of Wales was occupied; Gruffudd killed Robert of Rhuddlan at Deganwy on 3 July 1093. Drawn hatched; Cliopatria's Norman England takes the cells in 1094.

region.text: Gwynedd, 1085-1093 shape

ledger.note: 1099: Gruffudd ap Cynan recovers Anglesey and upper Gwynedd. He fled to Ireland in 1098 when the Normans reached Anglesey, then in 1098-1101 recovered Anglesey and upper Gwynedd up to the Conwy; the page says Welsh control was restored by 1100. Cliopatria's Gwynedd shape resumes in 1099. Cliopatria's 1099 shape omits four cells of the 1085 shape (Ruthin, Penllyn, Mawddwy, the upper Dyfi); no page removes them, so the 1085 shape returns whole (keyframe 1099).

region.text: the one cell round Bala (Penllyn) that Cliopatria's Gwynedd shape takes from its Powys shape in 1099

ledger.note: 1099: Cliopatria's Gwynedd shape takes one cell round Bala from its Powys shape. The page names no such change; it is a bridge to the shape. The same shape drops four cells of the 1085 shape (Ruthin, Penllyn, Mawddwy, the upper Dyfi) for which the page gives no event; they are kept here (keyframe 1099) and the Powys dossier, whose 1099 shape holds them, should be checked.

region.text: northern Ceredigion between the Dyfi and the Aeron (Llanfihangel, Aberystwyth, Llanbadarn): the Ceredigion cells of Cliopatria's 1210 Gwynedd shape that are not in the 1085 shape

ledger.note: 1136: Owain Gwynedd takes northern Ceredigion. The page: Owain 'invaded Norman-controlled Ceredigion, taking Llanfihangle, Aberystwyth, and Llanbadarn', in revenge for the execution of Gwenllian ferch Gruffudd ap Cynan; the Welsh then routed the Normans at Cardigan (Crug Mawr, late 1136). The Rhys ap Gruffydd page: 'Ceredigion was reclaimed from the Normans, but was annexed by Gwynedd'. Cliopatria never draws this hold (its Brythons and Powys rows cover the cells).

region.text: central Ceredigion round Ystrad Meurig, Lampeter and Castell Hywell: the Ceredigion cells south of the 1210 shape

ledger.note: 1137: the brothers take the castles of central Ceredigion. The page: 'When their father Gruffudd died in 1137, the brothers Owain and Cadwaladr were on a second campaign in Ceredigion and took the castles of Ystrad Meurig, Lampeter (Stephen's Castle), and Castell Hywell (Humphries Castle)'. Cardigan and the south-west are not drawn (Llywelyn takes them in 1215).

region.text: Tegeingl: the Flintshire cells (Mold, Holywell) of Cliopatria's 1216 Gwynedd shape; Rhuddlan's coastal cell is not in the land grid

ledger.note: 1146: Mold Castle in Tegeingl falls to Gwynedd. The page: news reached Owain in 1146 'that Mold Castle in Tegeingl had fallen to Gwynedd'; in 1148-1151 Owain had 'secured Rhuddlan Castle and all of Tegeingl from Chester' (the Owain Gwynedd page: he captured Rhuddlan about 1150). Cliopatria draws the Mold and Holywell cells as Powys until 1168, so the Powys and Powys Fadog dossiers overlap here. Counterpart: the Norman earls of Chester, within the English Crown.

union.text: northern Ceredigion between the Dyfi and the Aeron (Llanfihangel, Aberystwyth, Llanbadarn): the Ceredigion cells of Cliopatria's 1210 Gwynedd shape that are not in the 1085 shape
central Ceredigion round Ystrad Meurig, Lampeter and Castell Hywell: the Ceredigion cells south of the 1210 shape

region.text: Ceredigion, held for Gwynedd by Hywel ab Owain Gwynedd

ledger.note: 1153: Rhys and Maredudd drive Hywel out of Ceredigion. The Rhys ap Gruffydd page: 'Maredudd and Rhys drove Hywel ab Owain Gwynedd from Ceredigion by 1153', the region 'held by Gwynedd since 1136'; in 1156 Rhys feared an invasion by Owain 'in order to reclaim it for Gwynedd' and built a castle at Aberdyfi, but it never came. The year is the page's 'by 1153'; the Owain Gwynedd and Hywel ab Owain Gwynedd pages are silent on how Gwynedd lost Ceredigion.

region.text: Tegeingl: the Flintshire cells (Mold, Holywell) of Cliopatria's 1216 Gwynedd shape; Rhuddlan's coastal cell is not in the land grid

ledger.note: 1157: after Henry II's invasion Owain cedes Tegeingl. The page: 'Owain was to render homage and fealty to the King, and resign Tegeingl and Rhuddlan to Chester, and restore Cadwaladr to his possessions in Gwynedd'; the page dates the campaign to 1157 and gives no day for the settlement. The Owain Gwynedd page: he was 'obliged to surrender Rhuddlan and other conquests in the east'. Counterpart: Henry II's realm, to which Chester belonged.

region.text: Tegeingl: the Flintshire cells (Mold, Holywell) of Cliopatria's 1216 Gwynedd shape; Rhuddlan's coastal cell is not in the land grid

ledger.note: 1169: Tegeingl is back in Gwynedd. The page: 'Owain's army recovered Tegeingl for Gwynedd by 1169'. The Owain Gwynedd page has him 'recapturing Rhuddlan Castle in 1167 after a siege of three months', after Madog ap Maredudd's death in 1160 let him 'regain territory in the east'. The year is the page's 'by 1169'. Cliopatria draws these cells as Powys Fadog from 1169 (notes).

region.text: southern Powys and northern Ceredigion, the cells Cliopatria adds in 1210 (except three already in the 1085 shape)

ledger.note: 1208: Llywelyn annexes southern Powys and northern Ceredigion. The page: after John arrested Gwenwynwyn of Powys in October, Llywelyn annexed southern Powys and northern Ceredigion and rebuilt Aberystwyth Castle. Gwenwynwyn is driven out of southern Powys again in 1216. Cliopatria's shape grows in 1210. John's troops restore Gwenwynwyn to southern Powys in 1210 (ledger 1210); Llywelyn drives him out again in 1216 (ledger 1216).

region.text: southern Powys: the Powys cells that Cliopatria adds to Gwynedd in 1210 (the cells of Powys Wenwynwyn's shape), without the Ceredigion cells and without the cells already in the 1085 shape

ledger.note: 1210: John restores Gwenwynwyn in southern Powys. The page: 'John sent troops to help restore Gwenwynwyn to the rule of southern Powys'. The sentence carries no year; it stands in the 1210 narrative ('In 1210, relations between Llywelyn and King John deteriorated'; Deganwy) before the 1211 invasion. The northern Ceredigion that Llywelyn annexed in 1208 stays with him. Cliopatria keeps the cells in Gwynedd's shape from 1210, which the page does not support.

region.text: Tegeingl: the Flintshire cells (Mold, Holywell) of Cliopatria's 1216 Gwynedd shape; Rhuddlan's coastal cell is not in the land grid

ledger.note: 1211: John's invasion strips Llywelyn of Tegeingl. The page: 'In 1211, John invaded Gwynedd with the aid of almost all the other Welsh princes' and 'Llywelyn lost all his lands east of the River Conwy'. Of those lands this ledger draws the loss only for Tegeingl, the district it holds outside the 1085 shape; the 1085 shape's own cells east of the Conwy (Denbigh, Ruthin) stay Gwynedd's because Cliopatria draws them so and the page names no district.

region.text: the Perfeddwlad: Gwynedd Is Conwy, the lands between the Conwy and the Dee (Tegeingl, Rhos, Rhufoniog, Dyffryn Clwyd), as the cells of Cliopatria's 1216 shape east of the Conwy

ledger.note: 1212: Llywelyn recovers the Perfeddwlad. The page: in 1211 John invaded 'with the aid of almost all the other Welsh princes' and 'Llywelyn lost all his lands east of the River Conwy'; 'Llywelyn was able to recover all Gwynedd apart from the castles of Deganwy and Rhuddlan within two months in 1212', and 'in 1213, Llywelyn took the castles of Deganwy and Rhuddlan' (both castles lie in the east; their coastal cells are not in the land grid). The Perfeddwlad cells are Cliopatria's Powys Fadog until 1215 and Gwynedd's from 1216 (notes). Moved from 1213 to the page's dated 1212 sentence.

region.text: the south-west: Carmarthen, Kidwelly, Llanstephan, Cardigan and Cilgerran and the lands around them, with the Ceredigion cells from the Aeron to Lampeter that Llywelyn holds again: the cells Cliopatria adds in 1216 apart from the Perfeddwlad

ledger.note: 1215: Llywelyn takes the south-west. In December 1215 he led the lesser princes in taking Carmarthen, Kidwelly, Llanstephan, Cardigan and Cilgerran; Cliopatria's shape grows in 1216. Region widened to every cell Cliopatria adds in 1216 outside the Perfeddwlad (it had missed the Aberaeron cell); it includes central Ceredigion, lost in 1153.

1216: Llywelyn the Great proclaims the Principality of Wales at the Aberdyfi council. The Gwynedd page has him proclaim it; the Llywelyn the Great page says he never claimed 'Prince of Wales' and used princeps Norwalliae, then 'Prince of Aberffraw and Lord of Snowdon' from 1230. Same state, same colour.

region.text: the south-west: Carmarthen, Kidwelly, Llanstephan, Cardigan and Cilgerran and the lands around them, the cells Cliopatria adds in 1216

ledger.note: 1216: the lesser princes of the south and west do homage to Llywelyn. He held a council at Aberdyfi to settle the territorial claims of the lesser princes, who affirmed their homage to him; the 1218 Treaty of Worcester confirmed his conquests. Drawn in the lighter tint.

intersect.text: southern Powys: the Powys cells that Cliopatria adds to Gwynedd in 1210 (the cells of Powys Wenwynwyn's shape), without the Ceredigion cells and without the cells already in the 1085 shape

region.text: southern Powys as Cliopatria's 1216 and 1236 shapes both hold it (the Montgomery cell, in the 1216 shape only, and the Rhayader cell, which the 1234 Builth gain restores, are left out)

ledger.note: 1216: Llywelyn drives Gwenwynwyn out of southern Powys again. The page: after the Aberdyfi council of 1216 'Llywelyn called up the other princes for a campaign against him and drove him out of southern Powys once more'. Cliopatria's Gwynedd shape already holds the cells from 1210.

region.text: Builth (Buellt) and the upper Wye: the cells Cliopatria adds in 1236

ledger.note: 1234: Llywelyn holds Builth. The Peace of Middle (21 June 1234) gave a two-year truce, with Cardigan and Builth retained, after his 1231-1234 campaign through Montgomery, New Radnor, Hay, Brecon, Neath and Kidwelly. Cliopatria's shape grows in 1236.

region.text: the south-west: Carmarthen, Kidwelly, Llanstephan, Cardigan and Cilgerran and the lands around them, the cells Cliopatria adds in 1216

ledger.note: 1240: Llywelyn the Great dies at Aberconwy Abbey on 11 April and his overlordship lapses. David Moore: his supremacy was personal and left no institutional framework, so that it did not survive his death.

region.text: all his lands outside Gwynedd: the Perfeddwlad, Builth and the south

ledger.note: 1241: Dafydd submits to Henry III and gives up the lands beyond Gwynedd. In August Henry invaded and after a short campaign Dafydd was forced to submit, having to 'give up all his lands outside Gwynedd' (the Treaty of Gwern Eigron), among them his possessions in modern Flintshire.

intersect.text: the Perfeddwlad: Gwynedd Is Conwy, the lands between the Conwy and the Dee (Tegeingl, Rhos, Rhufoniog, Dyffryn Clwyd), as the cells of Cliopatria's 1216 shape east of the Conwy

region.text: Flintshire (Tegeingl), where Mold lay

ledger.note: 1245: Dafydd takes back Mold and Flintshire. After Gruffudd's death in March 1244 he allied with other Welsh princes to attack English possessions; by March 1245 he had recovered Mold and his former possessions in modern Flintshire. Henry invaded again in August 1245 and built Deganwy Castle.

intersect.text: the Perfeddwlad: Gwynedd Is Conwy, the lands between the Conwy and the Dee (Tegeingl, Rhos, Rhufoniog, Dyffryn Clwyd), as the cells of Cliopatria's 1216 shape east of the Conwy

region.text: Flintshire (Tegeingl), where Mold lay

ledger.note: 1247: the Treaty of Woodstock. In April Llywelyn and Owain, who had divided Gwynedd after Dafydd's death on 25 February 1246, 'came to terms with him at the cost of the loss of much territory' (the Llywelyn ap Gruffudd page: restricted to the west of the Conwy).

region.text: the Perfeddwlad: Gwynedd Is Conwy, the lands between the Conwy and the Dee (Tegeingl, Rhos, Rhufoniog, Dyffryn Clwyd), as the cells of Cliopatria's 1216 shape east of the Conwy

ledger.note: 1256: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd crosses the Conwy. After the Battle of Bryn Derwin (June 1255) made him sole ruler of Gwynedd west of the Conwy, 'by early December [1256], Llywelyn controlled all of Gwynedd Is Conwy, apart from the royal castle at Dyserth'.

union.text: the Perfeddwlad: Gwynedd Is Conwy, the lands between the Conwy and the Dee (Tegeingl, Rhos, Rhufoniog, Dyffryn Clwyd), as the cells of Cliopatria's 1216 shape east of the Conwy

region.text: the lands of Powys, Ceredigion and Carmarthenshire in Cliopatria's 1236 shape beyond Gwynedd proper and the Perfeddwlad, without Builth

ledger.note: 1257: Llywelyn sweeps south. He took lands in Gwrtheyrnion, driving out Roger Mortimer, then moved into Powys and Deheubarth, reaching the Bristol Channel; some local lords later returned to the English side.

1258: Llywelyn ap Gruffudd styles himself Prince of Wales. The page: 'In early 1258, Llywelyn was using the title Prince of Wales', first in an agreement with his supporters and Scottish nobles; the English Crown did not recognise it. Same state, same colour.

region.text: Dinefwr and the Tywi valley, the Carmarthenshire cells of Cliopatria's 1236 shape

ledger.note: 1259: Dinefwr becomes a vassal kingdom of Gwynedd. Llywelyn jailed Maredudd at Criccieth Castle until Christmas, after which Dinefwr became a vassal kingdom of Gwynedd. Drawn in the lighter tint. Counterpart is the slug deheubarth (the Dinefwr line); a dossier is requested.

region.text: Builth (Buellt) and the upper Wye: the cells Cliopatria adds in 1236

ledger.note: 1260: Llywelyn takes Buellt. In January 1260 he dislodged Roger Mortimer from Buellt and later took the Lordship of Brecon, where the local Welsh ousted their Marcher lord.

region.text: Powys Wenwynwyn, southern Powys

ledger.note: 1263: Gruffydd ap Gwenwynwyn of Powys Wenwynwyn does homage. On 12 December 1263 at Ystumanner he 'did homage and swore fealty' to Llywelyn and his lands were restored. Drawn in the lighter tint.

1267: Henry III recognises Llywelyn as Prince of Wales. The Treaty of Montgomery (29 September 1267) made him 'Prince of Wales' for homage and a payment of 24,000 marks; the Edwardian conquest page adds that Henry accepted his re-conquest of the Perfeddwlad. Same state, same colour.

region.text: Powys Wenwynwyn

ledger.note: 1274: Gruffydd ap Gwenwynwyn flees to England. A 1274 plot to kill Llywelyn involved his brother Dafydd and Gruffydd ap Gwenwynwyn; both fled to England, and Llywelyn refused homage at Chester in 1275.

region.text: the Perfeddwlad: Gwynedd Is Conwy, the lands between the Conwy and the Dee (Tegeingl, Rhos, Rhufoniog, Dyffryn Clwyd), as the cells of Cliopatria's 1216 shape east of the Conwy

ledger.note: 1277: the Treaty of Aberconwy strips Llywelyn of the Perfeddwlad. He kept only western Gwynedd (and the title Prince of Wales); Eastern Gwynedd was split between Edward and Dafydd ap Gruffudd (signed 9 November 1277, after Edward declared war in November 1276 and marched from Chester in July 1277).

union.text: the Perfeddwlad: Gwynedd Is Conwy, the lands between the Conwy and the Dee (Tegeingl, Rhos, Rhufoniog, Dyffryn Clwyd), as the cells of Cliopatria's 1216 shape east of the Conwy

region.text: the lands of Powys, Ceredigion and Carmarthenshire in Cliopatria's 1236 shape beyond Gwynedd proper and the Perfeddwlad, without Builth

ledger.note: 1277: the lands that had been tributary to Llywelyn became effectively Edward's under the same treaty.

region.text: Builth (Buellt) and the upper Wye: the cells Cliopatria adds in 1236

ledger.note: 1277: Builth and the upper Wye pass to Edward with the other tributary lands.

region.text: Dinefwr and the Tywi valley

ledger.note: 1277: Dinefwr leaves Llywelyn's overlordship with the other tributary lands of the Treaty of Aberconwy. Counterpart is the slug deheubarth (the Dinefwr line); a dossier is requested.

region.text: Gwynedd west of the Conwy

ledger.note: 1282: the last war for Gwynedd. War resumed after Dafydd rebelled (on Palm Sunday, the Llywelyn ap Gruffudd page says, at Hawarden); Gloucester was defeated at Llandeilo Fawr in June, the Welsh ambushed Luke de Tany at Moel-y-don on Anglesey on 6 November, and Llywelyn was killed at Orewin Bridge on 11 December 1282.

region.text: Gwynedd west of the Conwy

ledger.note: 1283: Dolwyddelan fell in January and Dafydd was captured in June; the contest ends with the conquest.

region.text: Gwynedd west of the Conwy: Anglesey, Caernarfonshire and Merioneth

ledger.note: 1283: Dafydd ap Gruffudd is captured and Welsh Gwynedd ends. The page: 'The conquest of Gwynedd was completed with the capture in June 1283 of Dafydd'; he was taken to Shrewsbury and executed that autumn; the Statute of Rhuddlan (1284) annexed the land to the English Crown and set up the Principality of Wales; the Gwynedd page ends the Aberffraw dynasty in 1283. Cliopatria keeps Gwynedd to 1284.

wars.name: Battle of Chester
wars.outcome: Gwynedd and Powys defeated by Northumbria; 'Chester and the Cheshire Plain passed to the Anglo-Saxons'.
wars.note: The page's year is 613; the Powys page gives 613 in its infobox and 616 in its text. Cliopatria keeps the Chester cell in Gwynedd's shape to 704, so no zone is written.

wars.name: Cadwallon's war on Northumbria
wars.outcome: Edwin besieged Cadwallon at Glannauc in 629; Cadwallon and Penda killed Edwin at Hatfield Chase (12 October 633) and held Northumbria for a year; Oswald killed Cadwallon at Heavenfield in 634.

wars.name: Viking and Mercian attacks on Rhodri Mawr
wars.outcome: The Dubgenti attacked Rhodri on Anglesey (Gueith Diu Sul in Mon, 877) and forced him to Ireland; he was killed by Ceolwulf of Mercia's forces in 878.
wars.note: The page notes Charles-Edwards's view that Ceolwulf had a free hand while the Great Heathen Army attacked Wessex; the Battle of the Conwy (c. 881) is 'revenge by God for Rhodri'.

wars.name: Hywel Dda's takeover of Gwynedd
wars.outcome: After Edmund of England beat Idwal Foel, Hywel Dda took Gwynedd and Powys (942); on his death in 950 the House of Aberffraw was restored.

wars.name: Gruffydd ap Llywelyn's conquest of Wales

zones.text: south Wales: the 47 cells Cliopatria adds in 1056 (Deheubarth, Brycheiniog, Gwent and Morgannwg)

wars.outcome: Gruffudd killed Gruffudd ap Rhydderch (1055), took Deheubarth, Morgannwg and Gwent and ruled all Wales until 1063.
wars.note: His 1056 Hereford raid and the peace with the English are on the same page; the Annals of Ulster put his death in 1064.

wars.name: Harold Godwinson's campaign against Gruffydd ap Llywelyn
wars.outcome: Harold struck at Rhuddlan in late 1062; in spring 1063 Tostig invaded the north and Harold's fleet the south; Gruffudd died in Snowdonia and Bleddyn and Rhiwallon were given Gwynedd and Powys.

wars.name: Norman invasion of Gwynedd
wars.outcome: Hugh of Chester's forces reached Llyn by 1090 and most of Wales was occupied by 1094; Gruffudd killed Robert of Rhuddlan at Deganwy (3 July 1093), fled to Ireland in 1098 and by 1101 Henry I recognised his claims to Anglesey, Llyn, Dunoding and Arllechwedd.

wars.name: Henry I's invasion of Gwynedd and Powys
wars.outcome: Gruffudd ap Cynan rendered homage and paid a fine but kept his lands.

wars.name: Henry II's invasions of Wales

zones.text: Tegeingl: the Flintshire cells (Mold, Holywell) of Cliopatria's 1216 Gwynedd shape; Rhuddlan's coastal cell is not in the land grid

wars.outcome: Henry's 1157 invasion ended with Owain doing homage and fealty to the King, resigning Tegeingl and Rhuddlan to Chester and restoring Cadwaladr to his Gwynedd possessions; after the 1163 revolt with Rhys ap Gruffydd Henry invaded again (1165, Owain Gwynedd page) and retreated in the rain in the Ceiriog valley, and Owain's army recovered Tegeingl by 1169.
wars.note: Ledger: 1157 loss and 1169 gain of Tegeingl. The Gwynedd page dates the revolt to 1163 and the retreat to no year; the Owain Gwynedd page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owain_Gwynedd) dates Henry's second invasion and the retreat in the rain to 1165, so the war runs to 1165.

wars.name: King John's invasion of Gwynedd

southern Powys: the Powys cells that Cliopatria adds to Gwynedd in 1210 (the cells of Powys Wenwynwyn's shape), without the Ceredigion cells and without the cells already in the 1085 shape

wars.outcome: John restored Gwenwynwyn to southern Powys (1210) and in 1211 invaded Gwynedd with the aid of almost all the other Welsh princes: Llywelyn lost all his lands east of the Conwy, then within two months in 1212 recovered all Gwynedd apart from the castles of Deganwy and Rhuddlan, which he took in 1213.
wars.note: Cliopatria's Powys Fadog row holds the same cells until 1215 (notes). Llywelyn drove Gwenwynwyn out of southern Powys again in 1216 (ledger).

wars.outcome: Hostilities with William Marshal from 1220; the Marshals retook Cardigan and Carmarthen in 1223; terms at Montgomery in October 1223 gave up his Shropshire conquests; in 1231-1234 he burnt Montgomery, New Radnor, Hay and Brecon, took Neath and Kidwelly and held Cardigan and Builth at the Peace of Middle (21 June 1234).

wars.name: Dafydd ap Llywelyn's wars with Henry III

wars.outcome: Gwern Eigron (August 1241) cost Dafydd his lands outside Gwynedd; he recovered Mold and Flintshire by March 1245; Henry reached the Conwy in August 1245; Dafydd died on 25 February 1246 and the Treaty of Woodstock (April 1247) cost his nephews much territory.

wars.outcome: Edward declared war in November 1276, marched from Chester in July 1277 and Llywelyn surrendered without a major battle; the Treaty of Aberconwy (9 November 1277) left him western Gwynedd.

wars.name: Edward I's conquest of Gwynedd
wars.outcome: Dafydd's revolt, Llywelyn's death at Orewin Bridge (11 December 1282), Dolwyddelan (January 1283) and Dafydd's capture (June 1283) ended Welsh-ruled Gwynedd; the Statute of Rhuddlan followed in 1284.

certainty.note: Welsh kingdom frontiers are approximate; the one line the pages call a boundary is Offa's Dyke on the Mercian side, whose date is not given, and it is still drawn soft.
The Treaty of Montgomery (1267) and the Treaty of Aberconwy (1277) fix Llywelyn's lands by named districts, the Conwy being the line after 1277; the frontier with the Marcher lordships stays soft.

notes: Cliopatria's Gwynedd row is one continuous state (kingdom to principality, Aberffraw line) so it is not split; the 1216-1283 'Principality of Wales' is kept as rename events. Window of 922-959: Cliopatria has no Gwynedd shape (its Seisyllwg row covers the cells from 922); the pages date Hywel Dda's takeover 942 and the restoration 950 only, so 922-941 and 950-959 are new keyframes and 942-949 has none (Gwynedd's land is Seisyllwg's; the Seisyllwg dossier should start the takeover in 942, not 922). Powys: this dossier takes Powys in 855 (Gwynedd page) while the Powys dossier has Cyngen die in 854/855 and the Powys land inside Gwynedd's shape in 1040-1062; from 1063 Powys is drawn by the Powys dossier and Gwynedd without it, whereas Cliopatria's Gwynedd shape keeps it to 1084. Perfeddwlad and Tegeingl (repair pass of 2026-10-25): Cliopatria's Powys Fadog row (1169-1215, 1,294 km2) holds the Mold and Holywell cells (Tegeingl) and the Corwen and Ruthin cells, and its Powys row holds them to 1168; the Gwynedd page has Tegeingl in Gwynedd 1146-1157 (Mold 1146, 'all of Tegeingl' from Chester by 1148-1151, resigned 1157) and again 'by 1169', so Tegeingl is written as Gwynedd land 1146-1156 and 1169-1210 and from 1212 (lost with 'all his lands east of the Conwy' in 1211, Llywelyn page); the Powys and Powys Fadog dossiers must give those cells up in those years. The rest of the Perfeddwlad beyond the 1085 shape (the Wrexham, Llangollen and Corwen cells, which are Powys Fadog's own ground) is written from 1212 only, because the Perfeddwlad page says Dafydd ab Owain held it after 1170 and Llywelyn took it in 1194 (Llywelyn page: 1195) but gives no cells. Ceredigion: Gwynedd held northern Ceredigion from 1136 and central Ceredigion from 1137 until Rhys and Maredudd drove Hywel ab Owain Gwynedd out 'by 1153' (Rhys ap Gruffydd page, the only page that dates the loss); Cliopatria never draws this hold. Southern Powys: the 1210 loss (John restores Gwenwynwyn; the sentence is undated on the page and stands in the 1210 narrative) and the 1216 gain are written against kingdom-of-powys-wenwynwyn; Cliopatria keeps the cells in Gwynedd from 1210. 1099-1168 shape: Cliopatria's 1099 shape drops four cells of the 1085 shape (Ruthin, Penllyn, Mawddwy, the upper Dyfi) and adds one Bala cell, with no page behind either; the dossier keeps the 1085 shape plus the Bala cell and records the Bala cell as a confidence-1 gain; the Gwynedd page dates Dyffryn Clwyd's vassalage to 1124 and Meirionnydd's firm hold to 1136, so the four cells may not have been firmly Gwynedd's before then, but the page names no other holder (the Powys dossier's 1099 shape holds them: overlap to check). The 1277-1283 shape is the 1085 shape. Cliopatria's 1216 shape holds one Montgomery cell that its 1236 shape drops, and the 1257-1259 keyframe holds Builth that the ledger gains in January 1260; the pages are silent on both. Pages silent: the 705 loss to Mercia, the 656 and 661 shape changes and the Chester cell after 613 (the Battle of Chester page, opened by the Powys dossier, says no land changed hands). The Gwynedd page is silent on Athelstan's overlordship; no vassal event is written for 927-930. 1245-1247 Flintshire is a contest, not a change of owner, because the page gives Dafydd 'recovered Mold' and no later date for its loss before Woodstock. Counterpart choices: Deheubarth has no Cliopatria row after 959 and the Brythons residual row holds its cells in 1055-1066, so the 1055 and 1063 south-Wales events name brythons; Gwent, Morgannwg and Brycheiniog are named by their own slugs; the Perfeddwlad events (1211, 1212, 1241, 1256, 1277) name kingdom-of-england; the 872 gain of Seisyllwg's cells names brythons (Cliopatria's Seisyllwg row starts in 878); Ceredigion is lost to deheubarth in 1153; Tegeingl is gained from norman-england in 1146 and from angevin-empire in 1169, lost to angevin-empire in 1157 as the Crown that held or took it. Counterparts needing dossiers: marcher-lordships (the Marcher lords, Mortimer, Marshal, Braose; Cliopatria lacks them), deheubarth (Dinefwr; Cliopatria's Seisyllwg stops in 959 and its Brythons row carries the south), principality-of-wales (1284 successor). Gazetteer: Perfeddwlad, Deheubarth, Builth, Deganwy, Rhuddlan, Aberffraw, Tegeingl, Lampeter, Aberystwyth are not in the gazetteer (central Ceredigion is a 16 km disk at 52.2N 4.05W); regions here are Cliopatria shapes and admin-1 names only.
